blocks.content: Two sibling topics in this module have already set up exactly the problem NAT solves. The ipv4-vs-ipv6 topic covered why public IPv4 addresses are genuinely scarce, and the public-vs-private-ip topic showed how every device on your home network gets its own private address that means nothing outside your home. NAT is the actual mechanism that bridges these two worlds together.

Network Address Translation lets an entire network full of devices, each with its own private address, share a single public IP address when talking to the outside internet. This topic covers exactly how that translation actually works, mechanically, not just conceptually.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015403895-833864556.png
blocks.alt: Many devices, each with their own private IP, all appear to the internet as a single shared public IP through NAT

blocks.content: 1. The Problem NAT Actually Solves

Public IPv4 addresses are genuinely scarce, as the ipv4-vs-ipv6 topic covered in full. But a typical home might have a dozen or more connected devices at once, phones, laptops, a smart TV, various smart home gadgets. How do all of them reach the internet when the household was only ever assigned one single public address by its internet provider?
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015405720-647464437.png
blocks.alt: Public IPv4 addresses are scarce, but a household can easily have a dozen connected devices needing internet access

blocks.content: 2. The Core Mechanism: Rewriting Addresses in Transit
blocks.text: 2. The Core Mechanism: Rewriting Addresses in Transit

blocks.content: When a device on your private network sends a packet out to the internet, the router running NAT rewrites that packet source address, swapping the device private IP for the router own public IP, before actually forwarding it onward. When a reply eventually comes back addressed to that public IP, the router looks up exactly which private device the original request actually came from, and delivers the reply to precisely that device.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015407302-638807514.png
blocks.alt: NAT rewrites the source address on the way out, and looks up the correct private device to deliver replies back to

blocks.content: 3. The Translation Table: How the Router Remembers
blocks.text: 3. The Translation Table: How the Router Remembers

blocks.content: To make this lookup actually work, the router keeps a translation table in memory, recording exactly which private device and port each outgoing connection came from, and which public facing port it was assigned for that specific connection. This table is what lets a reply arriving days, or even just milliseconds, later find its way back to the correct device.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015408888-471174657.png
blocks.alt: A NAT translation table records exactly which private device each outgoing connection actually belongs to

blocks.content: 4. Why Port Numbers Matter So Much Here
blocks.text: 4. Why Port Numbers Matter So Much Here

blocks.content: This is where the ports topic from the Transport Layer module becomes essential. If two different devices on your network both happen to use the exact same local source port at the same moment, the router assigns each one a DIFFERENT public facing port. This is exactly how the router can later distinguish which reply belongs to which device, even though both devices are hiding behind the exact same single public IP address.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015410798-158485407.png
blocks.alt: The router assigns different public facing ports to distinguish connections even from devices sharing the same local port

blocks.content: {"headers":["Private side","Public side, after NAT"],"rows":[["192.168.1.10, port 5000","Router public IP, port 6001"],["192.168.1.11, port 5000","Router public IP, port 6002"]]}

blocks.title: This is why NAT is sometimes called PAT
blocks.content: Because port numbers are so central to distinguishing between devices sharing one public IP, this specific, common form of NAT is often more precisely called Port Address Translation, though NAT remains the far more commonly used name in everyday conversation.
5. A Real World Analogy

An office with one shared main phone line captures this well. A receptionist answers every incoming call and routes it to the correct desk inside the building, while callers outside the office only ever see and dial the one shared main number, never anyone individual extension directly. NAT plays exactly the receptionist role for your network traffic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015414121-108719861.png
blocks.alt: A receptionist routing calls to the right desk while outside callers only see one shared number mirrors exactly what NAT does

blocks.content: 6. A Real Limitation: Unsolicited Inbound Traffic
blocks.text: 6. A Real Limitation: Unsolicited Inbound Traffic

blocks.content: NAT translation table only ever gets built from OUTGOING connections initiated by a device on your own network. If some device out on the internet tries to initiate contact with a private device directly, out of nowhere, it fails, since NAT has no existing mapping at all for traffic it never saw a matching outgoing request for.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015417720-727296297.png
blocks.alt: NAT has no mapping for unsolicited inbound traffic, so an outside device cannot simply reach in on its own

blocks.title: A real security side benefit, echoing the public-vs-private-ip topic
blocks.content: This default block on unsolicited inbound traffic is a genuine, practical security benefit, closely related to the reachability point already made in the public-vs-private-ip topic. It is a side effect of how NAT works, not a dedicated firewall, but it does real, useful work regardless.
7. When You Actually Want the Reverse: Port Forwarding
blocks.text: 7. When You Actually Want the Reverse: Port Forwarding

blocks.content: Sometimes you genuinely want an outside device to be able to reach something specific inside your network, hosting a personal game server, for instance. Port forwarding, a deliberate, manually configured form of NAT sometimes called destination NAT, explicitly tells the router to route incoming traffic on a specific port straight to one particular private device, overriding the default outbound only behavior on purpose.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015419266-437679508.png
blocks.alt: Regular NAT shares one public IP outbound; port forwarding deliberately routes specific inbound traffic to one chosen device

8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming NAT is a permanent fix for IPv4 address scarcity, when it is a genuine, effective workaround, IPv6 remains the actual long term solution, tying back to the ipv4-vs-ipv6 topic.","Assuming any device out on the internet can freely reach into your private network, when NAT specifically blocks unsolicited inbound traffic by default.","NAT rewrites private source addresses to a single shared public address for outgoing traffic.","A translation table, keyed heavily by port numbers, is what lets replies find their way back to the correct device.","Port forwarding deliberately overrides NAT default outbound only behavior when inbound access is genuinely needed."]
items: Assuming NAT is a permanent fix for IPv4 address scarcity, when it is a genuine, effective workaround, IPv6 remains the actual long term solution, tying back to the ipv4-vs-ipv6 topic.
Assuming any device out on the internet can freely reach into your private network, when NAT specifically blocks unsolicited inbound traffic by default.
NAT rewrites private source addresses to a single shared public address for outgoing traffic.
A translation table, keyed heavily by port numbers, is what lets replies find their way back to the correct device.
Port forwarding deliberately overrides NAT default outbound only behavior when inbound access is genuinely needed.
